lessons.title: Surface Preparation for African Climates
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 1: Surface Preparation for African Climates. This lesson is the foundation of every profitable painting and decorating job you will ever do. In Africa, surfaces behave differently from what many imported textbooks describe. We deal with intense UV radiation, seasonal harmattan dust, high humidity along the coast, heavy rains in the tropics, and extreme heat in the Sahel and semi-arid regions. If you skip or rush surface preparation, your topcoat will fail, and your reputation will suffer. The business-first principle here is simple: preparation is where you protect your profit margin. A failed paint job costs you twice - once to fix it and once in lost referrals. Let us start with assessing the substrate. Common surfaces in African buildings include cement plaster, sandcrete blocks, burnt clay bricks, mud bricks, concrete, timber, metal sheeting, and gypsum board. Each needs a different approach. For new cement plaster, the critical issue is alkalinity and moisture. Fresh cement can have a pH above 12 and can stay damp for weeks in humid coastal cities like Lagos, Accra, Mombasa, or Dar es Salaam. Test moisture with a simple plastic sheet taped to the wall for 24 hours, or use a moisture meter if you can afford one. Do not paint until the reading is below 12 to 14 percent for masonry. Neutralise alkalinity with a dilute acid wash only if you are trained, or better, use an alkali-resisting primer. In the market, ask for alkali-resisting primer, not just any sealer. For old painted surfaces, you must identify the existing coating. Is it emulsion, gloss enamel, textured coating, distemper, or whitewash? Distemper and whitewash are common in older government buildings, schools, and rural homes. These are water-soluble and must be completely removed with a scraper and water, otherwise your new paint will peel. Gloss enamel needs sanding to create a key, then a bonding primer. Emulsion in good condition can be washed, sanded lightly, and primed with a matching primer. Never paint gloss over emulsion or emulsion over gloss without the correct primer. That is a classic mistake that leads to flaking within one rainy season. Now let us talk about dust. Harmattan dust in West Africa and dry-season dust in Southern and East Africa will settle on your prepared surface and ruin adhesion. Always wipe down with a damp cloth or tack cloth immediately before priming. In dusty environments, work in small sections and keep the area covered. If you are working on a construction site, coordinate with other trades. Do not prepare a wall while masons are cutting blocks nearby. Schedule your preparation after the dusty work is done. For exterior surfaces, remove all loose material, efflorescence, mould, and mildew. Efflorescence is the white powdery deposit that appears on masonry. Brush it off dry, then wash with a mild acid solution or a proprietary efflorescence remover, rinse thoroughly, and allow to dry. Mould and mildew are common in humid coastal areas and after the rains. Treat with a fungicidal wash, not just bleach, because bleach kills surface mould but does not stop regrowth. Let the surface dry completely. For timber, preparation means sanding with the grain, filling defects with a suitable wood filler, and priming knots with knotting solution to prevent resin bleed. In Africa, termites and borers are a real threat. Treat timber with an insecticidal wood preservative before painting, especially for roof timbers, doors, and window frames. For metal, remove rust by wire brushing, sanding, or using a rust converter. Prime with a zinc-rich or red oxide primer. In coastal cities, salt spray accelerates rust, so use a high-performance primer and consider a two-coat system. Galvanised metal needs a special etch primer or a weathered surface before painting, otherwise the paint will not stick. Now let us discuss tools and materials. You need scrapers, wire brushes, sandpaper of various grits, filling knives, sponges, buckets, clean water, primers, fillers, fungicidal wash, and personal protective equipment. Do not underestimate PPE. Dust masks, goggles, gloves, and boots protect you and your workers. In many African markets, you can source these locally at competitive prices. Buy quality where it matters: primers and fillers. Cheap primers are a false economy. They fail, and you repaint at your own cost. Let us talk about filling and patching. Cracks in masonry should be cut into a V-shape, cleaned, and filled with a suitable patching compound or mortar. Do not just smear filler over a crack; it will crack again. For large holes, use a sand-cement mix or a proprietary repair mortar. For small holes and dents, use interior or exterior filler as appropriate. Allow filler to dry, then sand flush. For joints between different materials, use a flexible sealant or tape and jointing compound to accommodate movement. Movement cracks are common in African buildings due to thermal expansion and poor construction practices. Address them with flexible fillers, not rigid ones. Now let us consider the business side. Surface preparation takes time, and time is money. But skipping it costs more. Price your jobs to include proper preparation. Explain to clients why preparation matters. Show them photos of failed jobs caused by poor preparation. Offer a warranty that is conditional on proper preparation. This builds trust and justifies your price. In competitive markets, many painters cut corners on preparation to win jobs. Do not be that painter. Be the professional who does it right. You will win repeat business and referrals. Let us also talk about health and safety. Dust from sanding and scraping can contain silica, lead, and other harmful substances. Lead paint is still present in some older buildings. If you suspect lead paint, do not dry sand. Use wet sanding methods and wear appropriate respiratory protection. Dispose of waste responsibly. Do not dump paint waste into drains or water sources. In many African communities, water is scarce and precious. Be a responsible business. Now let us summarise the key steps. Step one: assess the substrate and identify the existing coating. Step two: test for moisture, alkalinity, and adhesion. Step three: remove loose material, dust, mould, and efflorescence. Step four: repair cracks and defects. Step five: sand and clean the surface. Step six: apply the correct primer. Step seven: inspect before topcoating. Each step is non-negotiable. Let me give you a practical example. A painter in Kumasi, Ghana, was asked to repaint a school block. The previous paint was peeling. He skipped preparation and just painted over the old surface. Within three months, the new paint peeled. The school refused to pay the balance. He lost money and the contract for other blocks. Another painter in the same city took time to scrape, sand, prime, and fill. His work lasted years. He now has a maintenance contract with the school. That is the difference preparation makes. In conclusion, surface preparation is not glamorous, but it is the backbone of our trade. Master it, and you will build a sustainable painting and decorating business in Africa. In the next lesson, we will look at choosing the right paints and materials for African conditions. Before you move on, complete this practical task: inspect a wall in your area, identify the substrate and existing coating, and write down the preparation steps you would take. This will help you apply what you have learned.

lessons.title: Choosing Paints and Materials for African Conditions
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 2: Choosing Paints and Materials for African Conditions. In this lesson, we will focus on selecting the right paints, primers, and sundries for the African environment. This is a business-critical skill because the wrong choice leads to callbacks, refunds, and damaged reputation. The right choice leads to durable finishes, happy clients, and repeat business. Let us begin with the basics of paint composition. Paint consists of binder, pigment, solvent or water, and additives. The binder determines the type of paint and its performance. In Africa, we commonly use emulsion paints, gloss enamels, satin finishes, textured coatings, and specialised coatings. Emulsion paints are water-based and are used for interior and exterior walls. They are breathable, easy to apply, and low odour. However, not all emulsions are equal. Cheap emulsions have low binder content and poor UV resistance. They fade quickly and chalk in strong sunlight. For exterior use in Africa, choose a premium acrylic emulsion with UV stabilisers and good weather resistance. Ask your supplier for the technical data sheet. If they cannot provide one, be cautious. Gloss enamels are solvent-based or water-based and are used for wood and metal. They are hard-wearing and washable. In coastal areas, choose enamels with anti-corrosive properties for metal. For wood, choose enamels that are flexible and resistant to cracking. Satin finishes are popular for interior walls and trim because they are washable and have a low sheen. They are a good choice for high-traffic areas like corridors, hospitals, and schools. Textured coatings are used to hide surface imperfections and provide a decorative finish. They are common in African homes and commercial buildings. Choose textured coatings that are weather-resistant and flexible. Now let us talk about primers. Primers are the bridge between the substrate and the topcoat. They improve adhesion, block stains, and neutralise alkalinity. For masonry, use an alkali-resisting primer. For wood, use a wood primer that seals and protects. For metal, use a zinc-rich or red oxide primer. For previously painted surfaces, use a bonding primer if the old coating is sound but glossy. For galvanised metal, use an etch primer. Never skip primer to save money. It is a false economy. Now let us discuss thinners and solvents. Using the wrong thinner can ruin a paint job. Always use the thinner recommended by the manufacturer. In many African markets, painters use kerosene or petrol as thinners. This is dangerous and can damage the paint film. It also voids the manufacturer warranty. Educate your clients and your workers on this point. Now let us talk about fillers and sealants. Use exterior-grade fillers for outside work and interior-grade for inside. Flexible sealants are essential for joints that move. In Africa, thermal movement is significant. A rigid filler will crack. Choose acrylic or silicone sealants depending on the substrate. Now let us consider the African climate in detail. UV radiation is intense in most of Africa. This causes fading, chalking, and degradation of paint films. Choose paints with UV inhibitors and lightfast pigments. Dark colours absorb more heat and degrade faster. In hot regions, lighter colours are better for exterior walls. They reflect heat and last longer. Humidity is high in coastal and tropical regions. This slows drying and can cause blistering if the surface is damp. Choose breathable paints for masonry and ensure adequate drying time between coats. In arid regions, low humidity causes paint to dry too quickly, leading to poor film formation. Add retarders if recommended by the manufacturer, or work in cooler hours. Rain is a major factor in tropical Africa. Exterior painting should be scheduled for the dry season. If you must paint in the rainy season, use paints that are rain-resistant after a short drying time. Protect freshly painted surfaces with tarpaulins or plastic sheeting. Dust and sand are common in the Sahel and desert regions. Dust can contaminate paint and ruin the finish. Keep containers closed and work in sheltered areas. Now let us talk about sourcing materials. In Africa, supply chains vary. In major cities, you can find international brands and local manufacturers. In rural areas, you may rely on local suppliers. Build relationships with reliable suppliers. Buy in bulk when you can get discounts. But do not buy more than you can use before the shelf life expires. Check expiry dates on all products. Store paint in a cool, dry place, away from direct sunlight. Do not store paint in extreme heat. Now let us discuss cost versus value. The cheapest paint is rarely the best value. Calculate the cost per square metre per year of service life. A cheap paint that lasts two years may cost more over ten years than an expensive paint that lasts eight years. Present this calculation to clients. It shows you are a professional, not just a brush for hire. Now let us talk about colour selection. Colour affects heat absorption, mood, and resale value. In hot climates, light colours are practical. In commercial spaces, brand colours matter. Use colour charts and sample pots. Always apply a sample patch and let it dry before the client approves. Do not rely on wet paint colour. It changes as it dries. Now let us consider specialised coatings. There are anti-mould paints for damp areas, anti-bacterial paints for hospitals and kitchens, fire-retardant paints for commercial buildings, and anti-graffiti coatings for public spaces. These are growing markets in Africa. If you can offer these specialised services, you can charge premium prices. Now let us talk about tools and equipment. Good brushes, rollers, sprayers, and sanders make the work faster and better. In Africa, you can buy locally made brushes and imported ones. Test them. A good brush holds its shape and does not shed bristles. Rollers should have the right nap for the surface. Sprayers are efficient for large jobs but require masking and ventilation. Invest in quality tools. They pay for themselves. Now let us discuss health and safety again. Paints and solvents can be harmful. Work in ventilated areas. Wear masks, gloves, and goggles. Do not eat or smoke while painting. Wash hands after work. Dispose of containers responsibly. Now let us talk about client communication. Explain the paint system you recommend and why. Give them options: good, better, best. Let them choose. Provide a written quotation that specifies the products, number of coats, and warranty. This protects you and builds trust. Now let us summarise the key points. Choose paints that match the climate and substrate. Use the correct primer. Use the correct thinner. Do not compromise on quality. Calculate cost over service life. Offer specialised coatings for premium markets. Communicate clearly with clients. Let me give you an example. A painter in Nairobi, Kenya, was asked to paint a hotel exterior. He chose a premium acrylic emulsion with UV inhibitors. He used an alkali-resisting primer and applied two topcoats. The hotel stayed looking fresh for years. He got a maintenance contract. Another painter used a cheap emulsion. It faded within a year. The hotel refused to pay and told other hotels. The first painter is now a preferred contractor. That is the power of choosing the right materials. In conclusion, choosing paints and materials is a strategic business decision. It affects your reputation, your profit, and your future. Master this lesson, and you will stand out in the African market. In the next lesson, we will look at application techniques for different surfaces. Before you move on, complete this task: visit a paint shop and compare three brands of exterior emulsion. Ask for technical data sheets and compare UV resistance, coverage, and warranty. This will build your product knowledge.

lessons.title: Application Techniques for Different Surfaces
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 3: Application Techniques for Different Surfaces. In this lesson, we will cover the practical skills of applying paint and decorative finishes to various surfaces found in African buildings. Good application is what separates a professional from an amateur. It affects the look, durability, and profitability of every job. Let us start with the basic principles. Always work from a clean, prepared surface. Always follow the manufacturer instructions. Always maintain a wet edge to avoid lap marks. Always apply the correct number of coats. Always allow adequate drying time. These principles apply to every surface. Now let us talk about masonry and plaster. This is the most common surface in African construction. Use a brush for cutting in and a roller for large areas. For textured surfaces, use a roller with a long nap. For smooth surfaces, use a short nap. Apply primer first. Then apply two topcoats. Do not try to cover in one thick coat. It will not dry properly and may crack. Work in sections. Do not let the paint dry before you finish a section. In hot weather, paint dries fast. Work quickly or add a retarder if recommended. For exterior masonry, paint when the wall is in shade. Painting in direct sun causes the paint to dry too fast and fail. Now let us talk about concrete floors. Use a floor paint or epoxy coating. Prepare the floor by grinding or acid etching to create a key. Apply primer, then two coats of floor paint. Allow proper curing time before allowing traffic. In Africa, concrete floors are common in garages, workshops, and commercial spaces. This is a profitable niche. Now let us talk about timber. Timber is used for doors, windows, roofs, and furniture. Sand with the grain. Fill defects. Prime knots. Apply primer. Then apply two topcoats. Use a brush for small areas and a roller for large flat areas. For a smooth finish, sand lightly between coats. For a high-gloss finish, use a fine brush and apply thin coats. In humid areas, use a wood primer that resists moisture. In termite-prone areas, treat timber before painting. Now let us talk about metal. Metal is used for roofs, gates, window frames, and railings. Remove rust and old paint. Apply primer. Then apply two topcoats. Use a brush for edges and a roller or sprayer for large areas. For corrugated metal, use a roller with a long nap or a sprayer. For intricate metalwork, use a brush. In coastal areas, use anti-corrosive primers and topcoats. Now let us talk about gypsum board and ceilings. Gypsum board is common in modern African buildings. Prepare joints with tape and jointing compound. Sand smooth. Apply a primer-sealer. Then apply two coats of emulsion. For ceilings, use a roller with an extension pole. Work carefully to avoid drips. Use a drop cloth to protect floors and furniture. Now let us talk about decorative finishes. These include sponging, rag rolling, stencilling, colour washing, and faux finishes. These are high-value services. They require practice and creativity. In Africa, there is growing demand for decorative finishes in hotels, restaurants, and upscale homes. Learn these skills and you can charge premium rates. Now let us talk about spray application. Sprayers are fast and give a smooth finish. They are ideal for large jobs like warehouses, factories, and estates. But they require masking, ventilation, and skill. Overspray can damage property. Always test the sprayer settings. Always wear respiratory protection. Now let us talk about rollers. Rollers come in different naps and materials. Use a synthetic roller for water-based paints and a natural roller for oil-based paints. Use a short nap for smooth surfaces and a long nap for rough surfaces. Do not overload the roller. It causes drips and uneven coverage. Now let us talk about brushes. Use a good quality brush. A good brush holds paint, spreads it evenly, and does not shed bristles. Use a cutting brush for edges and a wider brush for large areas. Clean brushes after use. Store them properly. Now let us talk about drying times. Drying times vary with temperature, humidity, and air movement. In hot, dry conditions, paint dries fast. In cool, humid conditions, it dries slowly. Always check the manufacturer data sheet. Do not apply a second coat before the first is dry. It causes blistering and poor adhesion. Now let us talk about common application problems and how to avoid them. Sagging or running happens when too much paint is applied. Apply thinner coats. Brush out runs immediately. Poor coverage happens when paint is over-thinned or the wrong roller is used. Use the correct thinner and roller. Lap marks happen when you paint over dried edges. Maintain a wet edge. Blistering happens when painting on a damp surface or in direct sun. Check moisture and work in shade. Peeling happens when the surface is poorly prepared or the wrong primer is used. Prepare properly and use the correct primer. Now let us talk about quality control. Inspect your work as you go. Check for missed spots, drips, and uneven coverage. Fix problems immediately. Do not leave them for the client to find. At the end of each day, clean up. Protect your work from dust and rain. Now let us talk about productivity. Time is money. Organise your tools and materials. Work in a logical sequence. Do not walk back and forth unnecessarily. Use the right tool for the job. Train your workers. Pay them fairly. A motivated team is more productive. Now let us talk about client relations. Keep the client informed. Show them progress. Explain any delays. Respect their property. Clean up after work. A happy client refers others. Now let us talk about pricing. Price by square metre or by the job. Include preparation, materials, labour, and profit. Do not underprice. It is better to lose a job than to work at a loss. Now let us summarise the key points. Prepare the surface. Use the right tools. Apply the correct number of coats. Maintain a wet edge. Check quality. Work safely. Communicate with clients. Price properly. Let me give you an example. A painter in Kampala, Uganda, was asked to paint a church. He used a sprayer for the large walls and brushes for the trim. He finished in half the time of his competitor. The church was happy and recommended him to other churches. He now specialises in large buildings. Another painter used only brushes and took twice as long. He lost money on the job. That is the power of using the right technique and tools. In conclusion, application techniques are the core skill of our trade. Master them, and you will deliver quality work, satisfy clients, and build a profitable business. In the next lesson, we will look at health, safety, and environmental responsibility. Before you move on, complete this task: practise cutting in on a wall corner and rolling a large area. Time yourself and check for lap marks. This will improve your skill and speed.

lessons.title: Health, Safety, and Environmental Responsibility
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 4: Health, Safety, and Environmental Responsibility. In this lesson, we will cover the critical topic of protecting yourself, your workers, your clients, and the environment while working in painting and decorating. In Africa, where regulations may be less enforced, it is your professional responsibility to set high standards. This is not just about compliance. It is about building a sustainable business that people trust. Let us start with the hazards. Paints, solvents, primers, and fillers contain chemicals that can harm your health. These include volatile organic compounds, lead, chromium, silica, and fungicides. Exposure can cause skin irritation, breathing problems, headaches, dizziness, and long-term organ damage. Dust from sanding and scraping can contain silica and lead. Lead paint is still present in older buildings in many African cities. If you disturb lead paint, you can poison yourself and the occupants. Now let us talk about personal protective equipment. PPE is your first line of defence. You need respiratory protection, eye protection, gloves, and protective clothing. For dusty work, use a dust mask or respirator. For solvent-based paints, use a respirator with organic vapour cartridges. For spraying, use a full-face respirator. Wear goggles to protect your eyes from splashes and dust. Wear gloves to protect your skin. Wear overalls and boots. Do not wear loose clothing that can get caught in machinery. Now let us talk about ventilation. Paint fumes can build up in enclosed spaces. Always ensure good ventilation. Open windows and doors. Use fans to move air. If you are spraying in an enclosed space, use a respirator and forced ventilation. Never paint in a sealed room without ventilation. Now let us talk about fire safety. Solvents are flammable. Keep them away from open flames, sparks, and hot surfaces. Do not smoke while painting. Store solvents in approved containers. Keep a fire extinguisher on site. Know how to use it. Now let us talk about safe work practices. Read the safety data sheet for every product you use. Follow the manufacturer instructions. Do not mix products unless the manufacturer says it is safe. Do not use petrol or kerosene as thinners. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while painting. Wash your hands and face after work. Change your clothes. Shower. Now let us talk about working at heights. Painting often involves ladders, scaffolds, and roofs. Falls are a major cause of injury and death in construction. Use a stable ladder. Do not overreach. Use a scaffold for high work. Wear a harness if working at height. Do not work alone on a roof. Now let us talk about electrical safety. Do not paint near live electrical wires. Turn off power before working near outlets and switches. Use insulated tools. Do not use water-based paints near electrical equipment unless the power is off. Now let us talk about manual handling. Paint buckets, scaffolding, and equipment can be heavy. Lift with your legs, not your back. Use trolleys and helpers. Do not carry more than you can safely handle. Now let us talk about first aid. Keep a first aid kit on site. Know how to treat cuts, burns, and chemical splashes. For chemical splashes in the eye, rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help. For skin contact, wash with soap and water. For inhalation, move to fresh air. Now let us talk about environmental responsibility. Paint waste, solvents, and containers can pollute soil and water. Do not dump waste into drains, rivers, or on the ground. Collect waste and dispose of it at approved facilities. Recycle containers where possible. Use water-based paints where suitable. They have lower environmental impact. Now let us talk about lead paint. If you suspect lead paint, test it. If it is lead, do not dry sand or dry scrape. Use wet methods. Wear a respirator. Cover the floor with plastic. Clean up with wet wipes. Dispose of waste as hazardous waste. Inform the client. Now let us talk about dust control. Sanding creates dust. Use dust extraction systems if available. Use wet sanding for lead paint. Cover furniture and floors with drop cloths. Clean up dust with a damp cloth, not a dry brush. Now let us talk about mould and mildew. Mould can cause allergies and respiratory problems. Treat mould with fungicidal wash. Wear a respirator. Fix the source of moisture. Do not just paint over mould. It will come back. Now let us talk about worker welfare. Your workers are your greatest asset. Provide PPE. Train them on safety. Pay them fairly. Provide clean water and shade. Do not expose them to hazardous conditions without protection. A safe team is a productive team. Now let us talk about client safety. Your clients and their families may be exposed to fumes and dust. Warn them. Advise them to stay away from work areas. Cover furniture and food. Ventilate after work. Do not leave paint and tools where children can reach them. Now let us talk about legal and insurance issues. In some African countries, there are regulations on waste disposal and worker safety. Know the law. Get insurance if you can. It protects you and your business. Now let us talk about reputation. A safe and responsible painter is trusted. Clients prefer to work with professionals who care about safety and the environment. This can be a competitive advantage. Now let us summarise the key points. Identify hazards. Use PPE. Ventilate. Work safely at heights. Handle chemicals safely. Dispose of waste responsibly. Protect workers and clients. Know the law. Build a reputation for safety. Let me give you an example. A painting company in Johannesburg, South Africa, implemented strict safety rules. They provided PPE, trained workers, and disposed of waste properly. They won contracts with corporate clients who valued safety. Another company ignored safety. A worker fell from a ladder and was injured. The company faced legal action and lost contracts. That is the difference safety makes. In conclusion, health, safety, and environmental responsibility are not optional. They are essential for a professional painting and decorating business in Africa. Master this lesson, and you will protect your health, your workers, your clients, and your business. In the next lesson, we will look at pricing, quoting, and business growth. Before you move on, complete this task: review your current work practices and identify three safety improvements you can make. Write them down and implement them on your next job.

lessons.title: Pricing, Quoting, and Business Growth
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 3, Lesson 5: Pricing, Quoting, and Business Growth. In this final lesson of Module 3, we will focus on the business side of painting and decorating. You have learned the technical skills. Now you need to turn those skills into a profitable, sustainable business. This lesson is about pricing your work correctly, preparing professional quotations, and growing your business in the African market. Let us start with the cost of doing business. Every job has direct costs and indirect costs. Direct costs include labour, paint, primers, fillers, sandpaper, brushes, rollers, masking tape, and transport. Indirect costs include rent, tools, vehicle maintenance, insurance, marketing, and your own salary. You must know your costs before you can price a job. Many painters underprice because they forget indirect costs. They work hard but never make a profit. Do not be that painter. Now let us talk about calculating paint quantities. Measure the area to be painted. Calculate the square metres. Check the coverage rate on the paint container. It is usually given in square metres per litre. Divide the area by the coverage rate to get the litres needed. Multiply by the number of coats. Add a contingency of 10 to 15 percent for waste and touch-ups. This prevents underordering and delays. Now let us talk about labour. Estimate how long the job will take. Consider preparation, priming, painting, and cleanup. Add time for drying between coats. Multiply the hours by your hourly rate. Your hourly rate should cover your labour cost and contribute to your profit. Do not forget to include your own time. Many small business owners do not pay themselves. That is not sustainable. Now let us talk about overhead. Add a percentage for overhead. This covers your indirect costs. A common figure is 10 to 20 percent. Adjust based on your actual costs. Now let us talk about profit. Profit is not a luxury. It is what allows you to reinvest, grow, and survive slow periods. Add a profit margin of 15 to 30 percent. The exact figure depends on the market, the competition, and the value you offer. Now let us talk about pricing methods. You can price by square metre, by the hour, or by the job. Square metre pricing is common for large painting jobs. Hourly pricing is common for small or uncertain jobs. Job pricing is common for decorating and specialised finishes. Choose the method that suits the job and the client. Now let us talk about preparing a quotation. A professional quotation includes your business name and contact details, the client name and address, the date, a description of the work, the products to be used, the number of coats, the price, the payment terms, the warranty, and the validity period. It should be clear, concise, and professional. Do not just give a verbal quote. Put it in writing. This protects you and the client. Now let us talk about payment terms. Ask for a deposit before starting work. This covers your initial material costs and shows the client is serious. A common deposit is 30 to 50 percent. Ask for progress payments on large jobs. Ask for the balance on completion. Do not let clients owe you money for months. It damages your cash flow. Now let us talk about contracts. For large jobs, use a written contract. It should specify the scope of work, the price, the payment schedule, the timeline, the warranty, and the dispute resolution process. If you cannot afford a lawyer, use a simple contract template. It is better than nothing. Now let us talk about warranties. Offer a warranty on your work. It builds trust. But make it conditional on proper use and maintenance. Do not offer a warranty that you cannot honour. Now let us talk about marketing. In Africa, word of mouth is powerful. Do excellent work. Ask satisfied clients for referrals. Ask for testimonials. Take before and after photos. Use social media. Create a simple website or a business page. Print business cards and flyers. Network with architects, builders, and property managers. Join local business associations. Now let us talk about branding. Choose a business name that is easy to remember. Create a simple logo. Use consistent colours and messaging. Wear branded clothing. Keep your vehicle clean and branded. Professional branding makes you look established and trustworthy. Now let us talk about customer service. Answer your phone. Return calls. Be on time. Be polite. Listen to the client. Solve problems quickly. Do not argue. A happy client is your best marketing. Now let us talk about managing your finances. Keep business and personal money separate. Open a business bank account. Record every income and expense. Use a simple bookkeeping app or notebook. Pay your taxes. Save for slow periods. Invest in tools and training. Now let us talk about growth strategies. You can grow by offering more services, such as decorative finishes, waterproofing

Practical Reference: Surface Preparation, Paints and Application for African Climates

This module gives you the exact reference values, mixing ratios and site checks you need to price, prepare and finish a job correctly the first time. In African markets, where humidity swings from 20% in the Sahel to over 90% on the coast, and where substrate temperatures can exceed 45Â°C in direct sun, guesswork destroys margins. Every figure below is drawn from published technical sources so you can defend your quote with evidence. Use this lesson alongside your pricing sheet: the data tables let you estimate material consumption, labour time and rework risk before you sign a contract.

Failure to read the site costs more than any other mistake in this trade. The table below links measurable site conditions to the failure they cause and the corrective action. Carry a moisture meter and a thermometer/hygrometer on every quotation visit.

Condition Acceptable range Failure if ignored Corrective action Source
Substrate moisture (masonry) < 16% (carbide meter) Blistering, peeling, efflorescence Delay painting; ventilate or use breathable primer WHO (2020)
Surface temperature 10â32Â°C Lap marks, poor adhesion, blistering Shade wall; paint early morning or evening FAO (1993)
Relative humidity < 85% during application and cure Slow cure, sagging, loss of gloss Reschedule; use dehumidifier in enclosed spaces WHO (2020)
Alkalinity of new render (pH) pH < 9 before topcoat Saponification, colour loss Apply alkali-resistant primer; wait 28 days FAO (1993)
Wind speed (exterior spray) < 15 km/h Overspray, uneven finish, waste Use brush/roller or erect windbreak Industry TDS
Dust / airborne sand None visible Grit in film, poor finish Dampen ground; stop work in dust storms FAO (1993)

â  SAFETY WARNING â CHEMICAL AND HEALTH HAZARD

Paints, thinners, primers and fillers contain volatile organic compounds (VOCs), lead (in older stock), isocyanates and biocides. In poorly ventilated rooms, VOC exposure can cause headaches, dizziness, respiratory irritation and long-term organ damage. WHO (2020) classifies several solvents as carcinogenic or reprotoxic. Always: work in cross-ventilated spaces or use a respirator rated for organic vapours; wear nitrile gloves and eye protection; never eat, drink or smoke on site; keep children and pregnant women away from wet paint; store solvents in sealed, labelled containers away from heat and direct sun; dispose of residues through approved hazardous-waste channels, never into drains or soil. If you feel dizzy, stop work immediately and move to fresh air. Report skin or respiratory reactions to a health worker and retain the product safety data sheet (SDS) on site.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Measure before you quote. Record substrate moisture (< 16%), pH (< 9), surface temperature (10â32Â°C) and humidity (< 85%) for every room or elevation.
  2. Confirm cure time. New cement render needs 28 days; skim filler needs 24â48 hours before sanding and painting.
  3. Prepare in order: remove loose material â wash and degrease â repair cracks â sand â dust off â prime.
  4. Match primer to substrate. Alkali-resistant for masonry, anti-corrosive for metal, wood primer for timber â never substitute to save cost.
  5. Calculate litres, not tins. Use Table 1 coverage figures plus 10% contingency; this protects your margin on porous walls.
  6. Check weather and timing. Avoid exterior work above 32Â°C, in wind over 15 km/h, or when rain is forecast within the recoat window.
  7. Protect the client's property. Mask floors, fittings and glass; photograph before and after for your portfolio and dispute protection.
  8. Document the SDS and warranty. Keep safety data sheets on site and give the client a written care and warranty note â this justifies premium pricing and generates referrals.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Building Materials and Construction Practices for Tropical Climates (free full text; covers render, moisture and finishes).
  • WHO â Guidelines for Safe Use of Paints and Coatings (2020) (free PDF; VOC and lead exposure limits).
  • WHO â Preventing Disease Through Healthy Environments: Lead in Paint (free report; relevant to older stock).
  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health in Construction (free guidance; PPE and chemical handling).
  • Penn State Extension â Paint and Coating Basics (free university extension resource; application and curing science).

Business takeaway: A painter who measures moisture, temperature and coverage before quoting wins the job at a fair price and finishes without rework. Rework eats 20â40% of profit on a typical residential contract. Use the tables above as your estimating sheet, keep the safety box visible on site, and hand the client the further reading list as a professional touch â it positions you as the expert who protects their building and their health.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for cutting in neat edges between a wall and ceiling without masking tape?
options: A) A 2 inch angled sash brush
B) A roller with a long nap
quiz.explanation: An angled sash brush gives control for cutting in clean lines along edges and corners.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a primer before painting bare wood?
options: B) To seal the surface and improve adhesion
C) To increase colour depth only
D) To act as a topcoat
quiz.explanation: Primer seals porous surfaces and helps the topcoat bond properly.

quiz.q: Which paint finish is generally most suitable for a bathroom ceiling?
quiz.explanation: Moisture resistant emulsion helps resist condensation and mould in humid areas.

quiz.q: What is the correct order for preparing a previously glossed door before repainting?
options: A) Paint then sand then clean
B) Clean then paint then sand
C) Prime then sand then clean
D) Clean, sand, dust off, then apply undercoat and topcoat
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes grease, sanding creates a key, and dusting prevents contamination before coating.

quiz.q: Which abrasive grade is most suitable for lightly keying old gloss paint before undercoat?
quiz.explanation: Fine abrasives key the surface without cutting through the existing paint film.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overloading a paintbrush with emulsion?
options: A) It makes the paint dry faster
B) It causes drips, runs and uneven coverage
quiz.explanation: Too much paint on the brush leads to drips, runs and an uneven finish.

quiz.q: What does the term cutting in mean in painting and decorating?
options: C) Painting neat edges and borders by hand
D) Removing old paint with a scraper
quiz.explanation: Cutting in means carefully painting straight edges and borders with a brush.

quiz.q: Which safety precaution is most important when using solvent based paint in an enclosed room?
options: B) Use a roller instead of a brush
C) Paint faster to finish sooner
D) Ensure good ventilation and wear suitable respiratory protection
quiz.explanation: Solvent vapours are harmful, so ventilation and respiratory protection are essential.

quiz.q: Which surface preparation step is most critical before painting exterior walls in hot African climates?
options: A) Applying a thick primer immediately
B) Removing dust, loose particles and efflorescence
D) Adding more water to the paint
quiz.explanation: Dust, loose particles and efflorescence prevent proper paint adhesion and must be removed first.

quiz.q: In coastal African regions, what is the main cause of rapid paint deterioration?
options: B) High salt content in the air
quiz.explanation: Salt-laden air accelerates corrosion and paint breakdown in coastal areas.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing old flaking paint from a rough masonry wall?
options: A) A wire brush and scraper
quiz.explanation: Wire brushes and scrapers physically remove flaking paint from rough surfaces.

quiz.q: Why should surfaces be tested for moisture before painting in African rainy seasons?
options: A) To choose the paint colour
B) To ensure paint will adhere and cure properly
quiz.explanation: High moisture content prevents proper adhesion and curing of paint.

quiz.q: Which paint type is most suitable for exterior walls in hot, sunny African climates?
options: A) Water-based emulsion with UV inhibitors
quiz.explanation: Water-based emulsions with UV inhibitors resist fading and heat damage.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using acrylic paint in African conditions?
options: B) It is flexible and weather resistant
quiz.explanation: Acrylic paint is flexible and resistant to weather, ideal for varied African climates.

quiz.q: Which additive helps paint resist fungal growth in humid African regions?
quiz.explanation: Fungicides prevent mould and mildew growth in humid conditions.

quiz.q: For painting metal roofs in hot climates, which coating is most appropriate?
quiz.explanation: Heat-reflective coatings reduce heat absorption and protect the roof.

quiz.q: What is the recommended technique for painting a textured wall in Africa?
options: A) Use a roller with a long nap
B) Use a fine brush only
quiz.explanation: A long nap roller covers textured surfaces evenly.

quiz.q: Which application method is most efficient for large interior walls?
quiz.explanation: Spray guns cover large areas quickly and evenly.

quiz.q: Why should painters avoid painting in direct sunlight in hot African conditions?
options: B) Paint dries too fast causing lap marks
quiz.explanation: Rapid drying in direct sun causes lap marks and poor finish.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of painting a room?
quiz.explanation: Painting ceiling first, then walls, then trim prevents drips on finished surfaces.

quiz.q: Which personal protective equipment is essential when sanding old paint?
quiz.explanation: Dust mask and goggles protect against dust and airborne particles.

quiz.q: How should paint waste be disposed of in an environmentally responsible way?
options: C) Take to a licensed waste facility
quiz.explanation: Licensed waste facilities handle paint waste safely and legally.

quiz.q: What is a health risk of prolonged exposure to paint fumes?
quiz.explanation: Paint fumes can cause respiratory issues with prolonged exposure.

quiz.q: Why is good ventilation important when painting indoors?
quiz.explanation: Ventilation reduces concentration of harmful fumes.

quiz.q: When quoting a painting job, what should be included?
quiz.explanation: A complete quote includes materials, labour, and overhead costs.

quiz.q: What is a common pricing mistake for new painters?
quiz.explanation: Underestimating time and materials leads to losses.

quiz.q: How can a painter grow their business in Africa?
options: B) Offer quality work and get referrals
quiz.explanation: Quality work and referrals build reputation and grow business.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a primer?
options: B) To seal the surface and improve adhesion
quiz.explanation: Primer seals surfaces and improves paint adhesion.

quiz.q: Which surface requires special preparation before painting?
quiz.explanation: New concrete needs curing and removal of alkali before painting.

quiz.q: What does the term cutting in refer to in painting?
options: B) Painting edges and corners with a brush
quiz.explanation: Cutting in is painting edges and corners neatly with a brush.
